extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and general readers of number theory
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook chapters presenting and proving classical number-theory results (binomial-coefficient properties, Fermat two-squares theorem, quadratic reciprocity, Wedderburn's theorem) with Book-style proofs and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for selecting a proof for the Book
rubrics_metrics.description: Which of the many proofs of a theorem 'belongs in the Book' — i.e., is the canonical, exemplary proof? The author asks whether the deciding factors should be the shortest proof, the most unexpected proof, or the proof with the greatest potential for generalization to deeper reciprocity laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: the question is raised in the introduction to the chapter on quadratic reciprocity. The author states they chose two proofs (based on Gauss' third and sixth proofs), motivating one as possibly the simplest and most pleasing and the other as a starting point for generalizations. This is an explicit, informal evaluative standard used by the author to select which proofs to present as 'Book Proofs.'
